'''Michael Levin'''  is an American [[developmental biology|developmental]] and [[synthetic biology|synthetic biologist]]. He is a professor of [[biomedical engineering]] and the Vannevar Bush Distinguished Professor of Biology at [[Tufts University]], where he is the director of the Allen Discovery Center and the Tufts Center for Regenerative and Developmental Biology.<ref name="tufts"/> He is also co-director of the Institute for Computationally Designed Organisms<ref name="ICDO">{{cite web |title=Institute for Computationally Designed Organisms|url=https://icdorgs.org/ |access-date=17 January 2022}}</ref> with [[Josh Bongard]].

==Early life==
Michael Levin was born in Moscow, USSR, in 1969, into a [[Jewish]] family.<ref name="theny">{{cite magazine |title=Persuading the Body to Regenerate Its Limbs |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/05/10/persuading-the-body-to-regenerate-its-limbs |magazine=The New Yorker|date=29 April 2021 }}</ref> His parents faced [[antisemitism in the Soviet Union]], and in 1978 took advantage of a visa program for Soviet Jews and moved the family to Lynn, Massachusetts.<ref name="theny"/> Levin's father was a computer programmer and worked for the Soviet weather service;<ref name="theny"/> his mother was a concert pianist.<ref name="oral-hist">{{cite web |title=Oral History Interviews with Michael Levin |date=24 September 2021 |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/44577 |publisher=American Institute of Physics}}</ref>

[[File:Michael Levin.jpg|thumb|Levin in 2014]]

Levin's family immigration was sponsored by Temple Sinai in [[Marblehead, Massachusetts]]. His family is still members of Temple Sinai.<ref name="oral-hist"/> Levin stated that "... I've always lived within about a mile radius of where we landed in '78."<ref name="oral-hist"/>

In 1986, at 17 years old, Levin read [[Robert O. Becker]]'s book ''[[The Body Electric (book)|The Body Electric]]'', which focused on the intersection between bioelectricity and medicine. This was something Levin said looked like "everything I was thinking about" at the time, discovering that the medical interest in electricity was thousands of years old. This would inspire his later interest and research into bioelectricity and related topics.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Moskvitch |first=Katia |date=2018-03-13 |title=Brainless Embryos Suggest Bioelectricity Guides Growth |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/brainless-embryos-suggest-bioelectricity-guides-growth-20180313/ |access-date=2026-05-06 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Hutson |first=Matthew |title=Persuading the Body to Regenerate Its Limbs |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/05/10/persuading-the-body-to-regenerate-its-limbs |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210505133009/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/05/10/persuading-the-body-to-regenerate-its-limbs |archive-date=2021-05-05 |access-date=2026-05-06 |work=The New Yorker |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Career==
Levin received dual [[bachelor's degree]]s in computer science and biology from Tufts University, and a [[Ph.D.]] in genetics from Harvard University (working in the lab of [[Clifford Tabin]]). His [[post-doctoral]] training was in the Cell Biology department of Harvard School of Medicine with [[Mark Mercola]].<ref name="Mark Mercola">{{cite web |title=Mark Mercola |date=19 March 2018 |url=https://biox.stanford.edu/people/mark-mercola |access-date=17 January 2022}}</ref> Levin first established his independent lab at the [[Forsyth Institute]] in 2000. His research interests include: bioelectrical signals by which cells communicate to serve the dynamic anatomical needs of the organism during development, regeneration, and cancer suppression; basal cognition and intelligence in diverse unconventional substrates; and top-down control of form and function across scales in biology. He moved his group to Tufts in 2009.<ref name="Levin_Lab">{{cite web |title=Levin Lab |url=https://ase.tufts.edu/biology/labs/levin/ |website=Tufts University: The Levin Lab |access-date=20 January 2022}}</ref> In 2010, he also became an associate member of the [[Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering]] at Harvard Medical School.<ref name="WI_Michael_Levin">{{cite web |title=Wyss Institute: Michael Levin |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/team/associate-faculty/michael-levin-ph-d/ |website=Wyss Institute: Michael Levin |date=28 March 2017 |access-date=20 January 2022}}</ref>

He was appointed to the Vannevar Bush endowed Chair in 2011 and received the IFESS Scientist of Vision Award in 2012.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-13 |title=Xenobots and Futures of Life |url=https://berggruen.org/news/xenobots-and-futures-of-life |access-date=2026-10-03 |website=www.berggruen.org |language=en-us}}</ref><ref name="biosketch">{{Cite web|url=https://ase.tufts.edu/biology/labs/levin/people/biosketch.pdf|title=Michael Levin Biographical Sketch|url-status=dead|website=tufts.edu|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190124043400/https://ase.tufts.edu/biology/labs/levin/people/biosketch.pdf|archive-date=2019-01-24}}</ref>

[[File:A xenobot in simulation and reality.png|thumb|A xenobot design discovered in simulation (left) and the deployed organism (right) built from frog skin (green) and heart muscle (red).]]

He is known for co-discovering [[xenobot]]s, "living robots made from frog skin cells [that] can sense their environment".<ref>{{cite news |title=Living robots made from frog skin cells can sense their environment |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2273516-living-robots-made-from-frog-skin-cells-can-sense-their-environment/ |publisher=New Scientist}}</ref> This research is focused on development of a multiplexed, microfluidic, ''[[Xenopus laevis|Xenopus]]'' embryo culture system that will enable discovery of new drug targets and development of therapeutics when combined with [[multiomics]] and an integrated [[bioinformatics]] pipeline. This work was funded by the [[DARPA]] L2M program.

As of 2021, Levin's lab is working on synthetic biology applications of [[bioelectricity]] for cellular control; development of a bioinformatics of shape, AI tools for discovery and testing of algorithmic models linking molecular-genetic data to [[morphogenesis]]; using techniques from AI, computational [[neuroscience]], and [[cognitive science]] to make models of morphogenesis.<ref>{{cite web |title=Levin's Lab: New directions |url=https://ase.tufts.edu/biology/labs/levin/research/newdirections.htm |access-date=7 June 2021}}</ref>

In 2004, Levin's work on the molecular basis of left-right asymmetry (Cell 1995) was chosen by the journal Nature as a "Milestone in Developmental Biology in the last century".<ref name="biosketch" /> Levin is co-editor in chief of ''Bioelectricity'', founding associate editor of ''Collective Intelligence'', and is on the editorial advisory board of ''[[Laterality (journal)|Laterality]]'' journals.<ref name="tufts"/>
